nameStory: The 'alpine' in Alpine Milkvetch tells you exactly where to look for this hardy little plant - high up in the mountains where few other flowers dare to bloom. The 'milkvetch' part comes from an old belief that these plants could help nursing animals produce more milk, though there's no scientific evidence for this claim.
description: Alpine Milkvetch is a low-growing perennial wildflower that hugs close to the ground in mountain environments. This compact plant rarely grows taller than 6 inches, forming small mats or cushions of divided leaves. It produces clusters of small, pea-like purple and white flowers that seem almost too delicate for such harsh, windswept locations. As a member of the legume family, it's related to beans and peas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pea-like flowers in drooping clusters, with purple-blue petals that fade to white or cream at the tips - like tiny purple and white flags waving in the mountain breeze

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves divided into 13-25 small oval leaflets that feel soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch, arranged like tiny green feathers along the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats rarely more than 6 inches tall, staying close to the ground as protection against harsh alpine winds

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, inflated seed pods that dangle from the stems and rattle softly when dry, containing several hard, dark seeds

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Stems are covered in fine, soft hairs that give them a grayish appearance and help protect the plant from cold mountain conditions

habitat: Alpine Milkvetch grows in the harsh, rocky environments of New England's highest peaks, particularly on Mount Washington and other summits in the White Mountains. Look for it in alpine zones above treeline, where it grows among rocks, in thin mountain soils, and on exposed ledges where constant wind and extreme temperature swings would kill most other plants.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges late in the season as snow melts, with fresh gray-green leaflets unfurling slowly in the short mountain growing season.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from June through August, when clusters of purple and white pea-like flowers appear and attract hardy mountain pollinators like alpine bumblebees.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and turn brown, rattling in the wind as they disperse seeds, while leaves may take on reddish tints before the early mountain winter.
seasonality.winter: Plants go dormant under deep snow cover, with only dried stems and seed pods occasionally visible above the snow on windswept ridges.

funFact: Alpine Milkvetch is one of the most widespread flowers on Earth, found not just in New England's mountains but circling the entire top of the world - from Alaska to Greenland to Siberia to Scandinavia - making it a true citizen of the Arctic and alpine zones everywhere.
confusionNotes: With only 16 recorded observations in New England, Alpine Milkvetch is rarely confused with anything simply because it's so uncommon and grows in such specialized habitat. If you think you've found it below treeline, you're probably looking at a different plant entirely.
contextualKnowledge: Don't be fooled by the name 'milkvetch' - this plant has nothing to do with increasing milk production and the old folk belief has been thoroughly debunked. The extreme rarity of this plant in New England (only 16 observations) makes every sighting scientifically valuable.
compareHints: Alpine Milkvetch differs from its cousin Canadian Milkvetch by being much shorter and growing only in alpine zones, while Canadian Milkvetch grows tall in lowland prairies and fields. Robbins' Milkvetch is also alpine but even rarer, and Chickpea Milkvetch has much larger, more inflated seed pods that really do look like tiny chickpeas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike Alpine Milkvetch which grows in high mountain areas, Robbins' Milkvetch is found at low elevations along rivers.
Canadian milkvetch is much more robust and tall than its rare New England relatives like Robbins' milkvetch, which is a tiny alpine plant, or Alpine milkvetch, which stays close to the ground.
Among New England's milkvetches, chickpea milkvetch is the most robust and bushy, staying under 3 feet tall.
